last_transition_reason: The proof is a complete direct verification from the stated definition of the Gaussian q-binomial coefficient. Under 0 <= r <= n, both r and n-r are nonnegative, so both defining expressions are legitimate. Substituting s = n-r into the formula gives [n choose n-r]_q = (q;q)_n / ((q;q)_{n-r}(q;q)_r), and commutativity of multiplication identifies this denominator with ((q;q)_r (q;q)_{n-r}), which is exactly the denominator for [n choose r]_q. Hence the two expressions are identical as polynomials in q. There is no reliance on the root theorem or other forbidden dependencies.
latest_nl_proof:
Fix integers n and r with 0 <= r <= n. Then r >= 0 and n-r >= 0, so both quantities [n choose r]_q and [n choose n-r]_q are defined by the given formula

[n choose s]_q := (q;q)_n / ((q;q)_s (q;q)_{n-s})

for the relevant values s=r and s=n-r.

Now compute directly from the definition:

[n choose n-r]_q
= (q;q)_n / ((q;q)_{n-r} (q;q)_{n-(n-r)})
= (q;q)_n / ((q;q)_{n-r} (q;q)_r).

Since multiplication is commutative,

(q;q)_{n-r} (q;q)_r = (q;q)_r (q;q)_{n-r}.

Therefore

[n choose n-r]_q
= (q;q)_n / ((q;q)_r (q;q)_{n-r})
= [n choose r]_q.

So the two defining expressions are identical. Hence the Gaussian q-binomial coefficient is symmetric under replacing r by n-r; in particular, [n choose r]_q = [n choose n-r]_q as polynomials in q.
role_in_parent: Moves each lower index to the first half of [0,n] without changing the quotient.
statement_nl: For all integers n and r with 0 <= r <= n, define the Gaussian q-binomial coefficient by [n choose r]_q := (q;q)_n / ((q;q)_r (q;q)_{n-r}), where (q;q)_m := product_{i=1}^m (1 - q^i) and (q;q)_0 := 1. Then [n choose r]_q = [n choose n-r]_q as polynomials in q.

domain_restrictions: Therefore n is automatically a nonnegative integer.
The quantities (q;q)_r, (q;q)_{n-r}, and (q;q)_n are only formed for nonnegative integer indices.
q is treated as a formal indeterminate, not as a quantified numeric variable.
statement_semantic_sketch.normalized_claim: For every pair of integers n and r with 0 <= r <= n, the Gaussian q-binomial coefficient is symmetric under replacing r by n-r; that is, the coefficient defined by the q-factorial ratio for r equals the one defined for n-r, as a polynomial in q.
quantifier_order: For all integers n and r, assume 0 <= r <= n.
For each nonnegative integer m, define (q;q)_m by the stated finite product, with (q;q)_0 equal to 1.
Then the q-binomial coefficient defined from these q-factorials satisfies the symmetry identity.
The equality is asserted as an identity of polynomials in q.
